newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican president denies he owes back taxes.
newsitem.headline: Mexican president denies he owes back taxes.

text.p: Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo on Wednesday denied charges from a leading opposition politician that he owed his own government several years of overdue taxes on a property in the resort city of Acapulco.
Diego Fernandez de Cevallos, who trailed Zedillo in the 1994 presidential race, made the charges during a live interview with Televisa television network late on Tuesday.
"It is a slander," Zedillo told reporters at the presidential residence of Los Pinos in a brief response, then referred to a statement issued earlier on Wednesday.
The statement from the president's office said the accusation was "false." It said Fernandez may have been confused over a condominium the president once agreed to buy.

The statement said Zedillo was to have taken over the property around the time of his inauguration in December 1994 but declined because of his presidential duties. Zedillo unexpectedly became a candidate during the 1994 campaign after his predecessor was assassinated.
The company owning the condominiums offered to keep the property for its own use during Zedillo's six-year term, covering all the costs in the meantime, the statement said.

Fernandez himself on Tuesday paid local authorities roughly 290,000 pesos ($36,000) in back taxes on a property in a posh residential district called Punta Diamante on the outskirts of the Pacific resort of Acapulco.

The ex-candidate of the conservative National Action Party (PAN), who had campaigned strongly against government corruption, was hurt by revelations last year that he had not paid taxes on his Acapulco house.

On Tuesday, he complained on a live television news programme that while his case had received widespread media attention, several members of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) also owed taxes in the same site.

"There are others who own property in this development ... (including) an important member of the Institutional Revolutionary Party. I'm not sure you want me to mention his name," Fernandez said on the 24 Horas news show.
"I should think so," replied veteran pro-government news anchor Jacobo Zabludovsky.
"Zedillo Ponce de Leon, Ernesto," said Fernandez.
When asked by Zabludovsky, visibly upset by the allegations, if the former candidate could prove the charges, he said: "Absolutely. I have seen the documents."

The Mexico City daily newspaper Reforma on Wednesday showed part of a document appearing to detail the tax status of the Acapulco property owned by Zedillo, but it was not clear whether there was any delinquency involved.
Mexico's president holds extreme powers for a single six-year term and is rarely held to public scrutiny while in office, even by the press and opposition politicians.
Zabludovsky's news programme is the most widely watched in Mexico. It shuns criticism of the president.
